# Instruments: make your own from recordings (`yinse:`)

Turn a set of single-note recordings into a small instrument muser plays like a built-in one. muser measures each note's
partials (frequency, starting level and phase, a fast and a slow decay, the beating between the strings of a course,
left/right level and phase), its attack noise in ten octave bands (how loud, how fast it dies, left/right), and how much
the other strings ring along. Partials need not be harmonics: the modes of a bell, a bar or a drum that are not whole
multiples of the pitch are measured too. The result is a JSON of numbers (about 200 KB for 40 notes), not audio. It suits
sounds that are struck or plucked and ring away by themselves: yangqin, guzheng, piano, harp, bells, mallets, drums.
Blown or bowed sounds that are held are extracted another way: see "Held instruments" below.

```bash
muser yinse extract ~/samples/yangqin/ -o yangqin.yinse.json --name "my yangqin"
muser yinse compare yangqin.yinse.json ~/samples/yangqin/      # how close it is, note by note
```

```json
{ "instrument": "yinse:yangqin.yinse.json" }
```

From an instrument muser can already play (an SFZ library you may use, a plugin, a built-in one), let muser play the notes itself:

```bash
muser yinse extract --from "sfz:Piano.sfz" --pitches 21-108/3 --velocities 0.3,0.6,0.9 --hold 6 -o piano.yinse.json --notes-dir piano-notes
muser yinse compare piano.yinse.json piano-notes/
```

`--from` also plays a short note per pitch to measure the dampers: a piano's notes then stop when released (the sustain pedal holds them), a yangqin's ring on.
Check the source's license before you share what you extract (see the library rules below).

## Built-in or extracted?

Both are muser's own (yinse) and are told apart by how they are written: a built-in is `yinse.strike.yangqin` (dots),
an extracted instrument is `yinse:strike/grand-piano` (a colon and a path). Use both; pick by what the part needs:

| | Built-in (`yinse.<how>.<name>`) | Extracted (`yinse:<file or library name>`) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A physical / modal model written in muser | Partial tables measured from recordings |
| Sounds like | The instrument in general | That recording of that instrument (closest to the real thing) |
| Pitches | Any, and the techniques bend and slide it far (guqin 按音 / 泛音 / 走手音, ±24 semitone bends) | Any (blended between recorded pitches); bends work, but the timbre does not follow a press or slide |
| Playing techniques | The built-in ones (`technique`, `tremolo`, `trill`, `flutter` …) | Only what was recorded and tagged (`articulation`), plus `tremolo` |
| Tuning the sound | Many `instrument_params` | Few: the sound is the recording's (`release`, `tremolo_rate`) |
| Held sounds (flute, erhu, voice) | Yes, with their techniques (flutter, slides, bow changes) | The sustained tone of winds, reeds, organs and strings (`--held`): dynamics, slurs and vibrato, no other techniques; not voice |
| Where | Always there | A file, or a library on `MUSER_YINSE_PATH` (`muser sounds list --kind yinse`) |

When a library has the instrument, prefer it for exposed solo parts that should sound like a real recording; prefer the
built-in one for techniques the recording does not have, wide slides, or when no library is installed.

## Libraries

Instruments shared in [muser-yinse](https://github.com/claw-works/muser-yinse) install with one command:

```bash
muser yinse search piano                 # what the repository has: spec, range, license
muser yinse install strike/grand-piano   # into this machine's yinse library
muser yinse list                         # what is installed (and on MUSER_YINSE_PATH)
muser yinse remove strike/grand-piano
```

Then write `"instrument": "yinse:strike/grand-piano"`. `install` also takes a `.yinse.json` file or URL (`--as <family>/<name>`),
and `--repo owner/name[@branch]`, a URL or a folder for another library. A whole library folder (a clone of muser-yinse, your own)
can be put on `MUSER_YINSE_PATH` instead (several with the path separator); `yinse:<family>/<name>` finds
`instruments/<family>/<name>/<name>.yinse.json` there, and a plain file path works too. `muser sounds list --kind yinse` (and the sound panel of
`muser view`) lists what the libraries on this machine have, with each one's source and license.

## Recordings

- One note per file (wav, flac, aiff, ogg or mp3), starting at the attack, ringing until it has died away (at least 2-3 s).
  Dry is best: reverb in the recording ends up in the decays. Up to 20 s of each note are analysed; where a partial sinks
  into the recording's noise floor its decay is taken from the part above it (weak partials that are in the noise almost
  at once follow the note's other partials), so a noisy recording does not turn into endless ringing.
- Pitch from the file name (`A4`, `Eb3`, `C#5`, `Cs5`, or a MIDI number such as `69`), otherwise it is measured from the sound.
- Velocity from the file name (`v80` and `vel100` on 0-127, `v0.7`, or `pp p mp mf f ff`); otherwise the files of one pitch are
  ordered from soft to loud. One recording every 3-5 semitones and 2-3 velocities is enough: notes in between are blended
  from the nearest recorded pitches and velocities.

## How many notes to record

Not every key at every velocity: notes in between are blended. Extracting a piano from parts of its 90 recordings
(every 3 semitones × 3 velocities) and comparing against all of them:

| recorded | notes | spectral difference | level difference (mean) |
|---|---|---|---|
| every 3 semitones × 3 velocities | 90 | 2.66 dB | 1.2 dB |
| every 3 semitones × 2 velocities | 60 | 2.87 dB | 2.0 dB |
| every 3 semitones × 1 velocity | 30 | 3.10 dB | 3.8 dB |
| every 6 semitones × 3 velocities | 45 | 3.46 dB | 2.1 dB |
| every 12 semitones × 1 velocity | 8 | 4.12 dB | 4.3 dB |

More pitches make the timbre right, more velocities make the loudness right (with one velocity, soft and loud are the
same sound turned down and up). Advice: a pitch every 3 semitones at 2-3 velocities (at least 3 dB apart) on wide
instruments like the piano; every string or bar on instruments with few (guzheng, guqin, yangqin, marimba); always the
lowest and highest note. Then `muser yinse compare --between`: if its "between" number is much worse than the spectral
difference, record more pitches next to the worst ones. The full guide is in the muser-yinse repository
([docs/extracting.md](https://github.com/claw-works/muser-yinse/blob/main/docs/extracting.md); making a whole set from a sample
library and fixing an extraction that sounds wrong: [docs/refining.md](https://github.com/claw-works/muser-yinse/blob/main/docs/refining.md)).

## From one take (`--split`)

Instead of cutting the notes apart yourself, record the whole sampling session as one file and let muser find the notes:

```bash
muser yinse extract take.wav --split --notes-dir take-notes -o guzheng.yinse.json --name "my guzheng"
muser yinse compare --between guzheng.yinse.json take-notes/
```

It prints every note it found (time, length, measured pitch, level) and whether it was used or why not. What the take needs:

- A sampling take, not a piece of music: one note at a time, one after another, in any order. No chords, nothing played
  over a note that is still ringing.
- Let each note ring until it has died away before the next. A note is used only when the one before it has fallen 20 dB
  below it and it rings at least 0.5 s before the next; what is left of its decay after the next note starts is not
  measured, so longer is better (up to 20 s). Do not stop the strings by hand: that would be measured as the decay.
- A clear pitch between C1 and E7: the pitch is measured, not named. Bells, bars and drums (partials that are not harmonics)
  need one file per note with the pitch in the name instead.
- For velocity layers play each pitch two or three times: soft, medium, loud, at least 3 dB apart. Takes of a pitch within
  3 dB of each other count as one velocity (the longer is used); of more than three, the softest, middle and loudest are used.
- Quiet between the notes: a cough or a chair is taken for a note (it is skipped for having no pitch, but it cuts the note
  before it short). A steady hum or hiss is fine.
- Several takes can be given at once (same microphones and gain), e.g. one per register.

`--notes-dir` keeps the cut notes, named by pitch (`A3_f1t12.34.wav`: file 1, 12.34 s in). Listen to a few; delete a bad one,
rename a wrong pitch, add `_mute` or `_v40` to a name, drop in tremolo / vibrato / damp recordings, then run `extract` on
that folder (without `--split`) to rebuild. A solo performance mostly fails the rules above (in two solo recordings tried,
about 1 note in 100 passed and the result was poor): record a sampling take.

## Articulations (演奏法)

Tag recordings in the file name and they become playing techniques of the instrument; a note picks one with
`"articulation": "<name>"`. `muser instruments yinse:<file>` lists what an instrument has; a name it lacks fails validation.

- **Sounds**: `mute` (闷音, `muted` too), `harmonic`, `back` (反竹), `pluck`, `staccato`, `rim`, `soft`, `hard`, or any name as
  `art-<name>` (`A4_art-fanzhu_v90.wav`). Each gets its own partial tables from its own recordings (a few pitches are enough;
  pitches in between blend as usual).
- **Gestures**, measured from one or more recordings and applied to the plain sound:
  - `tremolo` (轮音): a recording of a tremolo gives strokes per second, how loud the other hammer is, and whether it speeds up.
    Then `"articulation": "tremolo"` (or `"tremolo": true`) plays every tremolo that way.
  - `vibrato` (揉音): a recording of a note with vibrato gives its depth (cents), rate and delay; `"articulation": "vibrato"` on a note.
  - `damp` (止音): a note struck and then stopped gives how fast it is stopped; `"articulation": "damp"` (or `"damp": true`).
  Gesture recordings are only measured, never used as sounds, so the instrument also needs plain notes.

```text
A4_v80.wav  A4_v80_mute.wav  D5_tremolo.wav  A4_vibrato.wav  E4_damp.wav
```

## Playing it

- Notes ring on after they end (no dampers); set `"release": 0.3` in `instrument_params` to damp them. For an instrument
  whose notes are always stopped when they end (bass guitar), extract with `--release 0.2`: that becomes its default.
- After extracting, every recording is played on the result and compared: a note that came out too loud or soft is
  corrected, and one that rings much longer than its recording (very short sounds: dead notes, staccato) is shortened.
- `"tremolo": true` on a note plays it as a tremolo (`tremolo_rate` strokes a second); `bend` works on every note.
- It is not level-calibrated: it plays as loud as the recordings would on an audio track. Check with `muser mix-report`.
- `compare` plays every recording's pitch, velocity and articulation on the extracted instrument and prints the spectral
  difference (third-octave bands, first 2 s, loudness matched; around 2-3 dB is close), the level difference (extracted
  minus recording, not matched: a velocity layer that is too loud or soft shows here), the decay at 0.1 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 s and
  the stereo correlation, beside the recording's. `--between` also takes each recorded pitch out of the instrument, plays
  it blended from its neighbours and compares that with the recording: how far off the pitches you did not record are.
  If that is much worse than the first number, record more pitches.
- Tables are version 2 (harmonic numbers, start phases, noise bands). Version 1 files still play; a muser older than the
  file's version asks to be updated.

## Held instruments (`--held`): blown and bowed

A sax, flute, xiao, organ or bowed string does not ring away: it sounds as long as it is blown or bowed, so what is
measured is different. From long notes (one per file, 2 s or more of steady tone without vibrato, every 2-3 semitones,
two or three dynamics each, named `A2_p.wav` `A2_f.wav` `C4_v100.wav`):

```bash
muser yinse extract --held ~/samples/my-sax/ -o my-sax.yinse.json --name "My sax"
muser yinse compare my-sax.yinse.json ~/samples/my-sax/
muser yinse install my-sax.yinse.json --as blow/my-sax        # -> "instrument": "yinse:blow/my-sax"
```

- Per pitch and dynamic: the fundamental, every harmonic's level and its phase against the fundamental (the shape of the
  waveform: the same spectrum with other phases sounds more electronic), the noise between the harmonics in ten bands
  (breath, bow hair), and how much the level and pitch of a held note wander. From the start and end of the recordings:
  how fast a note speaks, how much louder its first moment is, how fast it stops.
- From an SFZ library, a plugin or a built-in instrument: `--from "sfz:…" --pitches 37-68 --velocities 0.3,0.9 --hold 3`.
  When the library's dynamics are a controller, not velocity, name the layers:
  `--layers '[{"at": 0.24, "params": {"cc": {"1": 30}}}, {"at": 1.0, "params": {"cc": {"1": 127}}}]'`.
- `--poly`: the instrument plays chords (organ, ensemble). The default is a solo instrument: a note that starts before
  the last one ends is slurred (no new attack). `--glide 0.05`: how fast a slur reaches the next pitch (a wind changes
  fingering at once, the default 0.005; a string player's finger slides). `--vibrato 12,5.5,0.2`: the instrument's usual
  vibrato (cents, Hz, seconds of delay) as the default of its `vibrato_*` parameters; without it the vibrato measured in the
  recordings is used (notes with vibrato are straightened before they are measured), or none if they are straight.
  `--ensemble 4`: the recordings are a section in unison: every note is played by four voices slightly apart in pitch.
  `--strokes <folder>`: short strokes of the same instrument (spiccato, staccato): the timbre still comes from the long
  notes, the attack, decay and length of a stroke from these, and every note of the instrument is one such stroke.
  A solo instrument plays chords with `"solo": 0` in `instrument_params` (a section of horns).

Playing it (`instrument_params`, all automatable): `dynamics` 0-1 moves the timbre between the measured layers (soft is
darker, loud brighter) and can swell within a note; without it each note's velocity does. `vibrato_depth` (cents),
`vibrato_rate`, `vibrato_delay`; `attack` / `release` (multiples of the measured ones); `glide`; `breath` (the noise);
`wobble` (the unsteadiness of a held note, 0 dead straight). The held tone comes out within 1-2 dB of the recordings.
Library instruments made this way: `yinse:blow/karoryfer/bear-sax` (baritone saxophone), `yinse:blow/cloudbeer/bangdi`,
`qudi` and `xiao` (the sustained tone of muser's built-in flutes as tables).
Every held instrument plays the per-note techniques: `flutter` or `tremolo` (flutter tongue on winds, a bowed tremolo on
strings), `slide` (a slurred note glides in), `trill` / `half_trill`, `scoop` / `fall`, `bend`, `accent`, and harmonics
(`"technique": "harmonic"`, optionally `"harmonic": 2-8` for the node: the note sounds at its written pitch). Bowed
instruments take a new bow stroke per note; put slurred notes on a track with `"solo": 1`. `--tremolo` extracts an
instrument from recordings of bowed tremolo (every note is played that way); `--poly` makes every note a new attack (organ,
solo strings). Stereo recordings give a stereo instrument.
Not there yet: note transitions are a rule, not measured; vibrato does not change the timbre; only the sustained tone
(no staccato, flutter or harmonics); outside the recorded range the nearest note is stretched.

## Percussion kits (`--kit`)

A drum kit is extracted from single hits: every piece struck alone, one hit per file, at a few velocities (three to five;
the same microphones and gain for all of them, dry, each hit left to ring out).

```bash
muser yinse extract --kit ~/samples/my-kit/ -o my-kit.yinse.json --name "My kit"
muser yinse compare my-kit.yinse.json ~/samples/my-kit/       # hit by hit
muser yinse install my-kit.yinse.json                         # -> "instrument": "yinse:kit/my-kit"
```

- File names: `<piece>_v<velocity>.wav`: `kick_v100.wav`, `snare_v60.wav`, `open_hat_mf.wav`. The piece is a GM name
  (kick, snare, side_stick, clap, closed_hat, pedal_hat, open_hat, tom_low … crash, ride, ride_bell, tambourine, cowbell …,
  the names in drums.md) or starts with its key: `49_big_gong_ff.wav`. Velocity is `v80` / `vel100` (0-127), `v0.7` or
  `pp` … `ff`; without it the hits of a piece are ordered by loudness. `rr2` (round robin) is ignored: several hits at
  one velocity are averaged in the velocity table.
- A `kit.json` in the folder can name things: `{ "name": "My kit", "pieces": { "big_gong": { "key": 49, "keys": [49, 50],
  "zh": "大锣", "chokes": [49] } } }`. Without it the closed (42) and pedal (44) hi-hats choke the open one (46).
- From an SFZ drum library, a plugin or a built-in kit instead of files: `--from "sfz:/path/kit.sfz" --keys 35-59
  --velocities 0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.95` plays every key at every velocity (silent keys are skipped); `--params` passes
  `instrument_params` (an SFZ's `{"cc": {"4": 127}}` to close its hi-hat), `--notes-dir` keeps the hits for `compare`.
- `--fallback drums.acoustic`: keys the kit does not have are played by that built-in kit.

What is measured, from the loudest hit of each piece: the resonances as damped sinusoids (frequency, level, decay, start
phase, left and right; found one by one, each subtracted before the next is looked for, so a drum's thump is rebuilt
from a dozen or two of them and the waveform matches, not only the spectrum), a pitch glide of the lowest resonance (kick, toms, gongs), the
noise that is left in ten bands (a fast and a slow decay each: cymbals, snare wires, the stick), pan and stereo width.

Velocity layers: a piece recorded at several velocities gets up to three layers (the softest, the loudest and the one in the
middle), each measured as above: a soft stroke is its own sound (a slacker head, another pitch and waveform, hardly any
stick), not the loud one turned down. A velocity between two layers plays both, cross-faded, at the level the recordings
have at that velocity (the levels of all the recorded velocities are kept, also of those that did not become a layer). So
record at least three velocities per piece; five place the levels in between better. A piece with one velocity has one
timbre whose level follows velocity. The kit's level is calibrated on a kick / snare / closed-hat pattern.

What to expect: drums and short percussion come out close (1-3 dB spectral difference, and the first 150 ms of a loud
kick, tom or conga correlate 0.9 and more with the recording); cymbals are a sheet of band noise around a few dozen
resonances (5-7 dB on this measure, which cannot go much lower for noise-like sounds). With velocity layers a soft kick or
tom matches its recording's waveform as well as a loud one. It does not
suit rattles and sustained sounds (vibraslap, guiro, whistles, cuica, rolls): leave those to the fallback kit. Hits picked
out of an ensemble recording, or a kit that needs a body and a stick layer tuned separately, are still fitted by hand and
saved in the same format (`muser-yinse-kit`: pieces, each with parts of modes and noise layers and their velocity curves,
or with velocity layers; chokes, EQ, a kit compressor).
